# ICI Rechallenge in Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)

## Definition
ICI rechallenge in HCC is defined as the readministration of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy after either treatment failure or interruption of an initial ICI regimen [P3]. It has emerged as a novel investigational approach in HCC immunotherapy for patients who discontinue initial immunotherapy due to disease progression, immune-related adverse events (irAEs), or treatment completion [P2].

## Clinical Context and Rationale
ICI therapy is a cornerstone treatment for advanced HCC, acting by potentiating T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity through blockade of PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 [P3]. However, many responders ultimately require discontinuation due to progressive disease, irAEs, protocol-defined treatment completion, or other reasons, and subsequent therapeutic options remain extremely limited [P3]. In this setting, ICI rechallenge offers an opportunity to achieve additional clinical benefit after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation [P1][P2]. The biological rationale involves renewed immune activation potentially arising from immunogenic cell death, tumor microenvironment remodeling, and re-expression of inhibitory checkpoints such as PD-L1 or CTLA-4 [P2]. Mechanistically, three proposed pathways underlie successful rechallenge: (1) combining targeted therapy with anti-PD-L1, (2) switching between anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1, and (3) dual immunotherapy with CTLA-4 and PD-(L)1 inhibitors [P8]. For example, a rechallenge regimen combining targeted therapy and anti-PD-L1 in patients previously treated with anti-PD-1 may involve, at least in part, the first and second mechanisms [P8].

## Current Evidence
Existing clinical evidence comprises 10 retrospective studies, 2 prospective studies, and 11 case reports, collectively encompassing 383 HCC patients with prior ICI exposure [P3]. ICI rechallenge achieved an objective response rate (ORR) of 13.8%, disease control rate (DCR) of 50.7%, median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 2.0–5.6 months, and median overall survival (mOS) of 7.4–16.7 months [P3][F2]. These outcomes are lower than those of initial ICI treatment (ORR 20.3%, DCR 69.0%, mPFS 3.7–5.4 months), possibly attributable to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge [P3][F2]. Notably, some studies reported enhanced responses after rechallenge compared to initial therapy (e.g., ORR 26% vs. 22% [Scheiner et al.]; 22% vs. 6% [Alden et al.]) [P3].

## Safety
During ICI rechallenge, irAEs occurred in 54.1% and grade ≥3 irAEs in 19.5% of patients, compared with 38.0% and 8.0% during initial ICI treatment [P4][F3]. Despite this higher incidence, only 1 (0.3%) fatal irAE was reported across the included studies, lower than the 3.1% following initial ICI treatment [P4]. Most irAEs were manageable with ICI discontinuation, corticosteroids, and other approaches [P4]. Prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication to rechallenge but warrant close monitoring and individualized risk-benefit assessment [P5].

## Patient Selection
Favorable outcomes appear more frequent in patients with preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI grades 1–2), age ≤60 years, and lower tumor burden [P2][P5]. An initial best overall response of PD is not a contraindication for rechallenge [P5].

## Limitations and Future Directions
No standardized rechallenge regimen, patient indications, or treatment protocols currently exist, and clinical decisions are guided primarily by empirical considerations [P2][P3]. The pooled efficacy data represent an overall view across heterogeneous studies without an optimal indication or treatment strategy [P3]. Although ICI rechallenge has shown efficacy and acceptable safety in certain HCC patients, many clinical and scientific questions remain unresolved [P7]. Future research should focus on optimizing and expanding treatment regimens (e.g., novel ICIs such as anti-TIGIT, anti-LAG3, or bispecific antibodies; tumor stroma modulators; combination with local treatments), refining rechallenge timing, improving patient selection, and developing response biomarkers [P7].

## Note on Cited Reference Material
The reference list includes supporting citations on ICI rechallenge in other malignancies, such as advanced melanoma [P6], which are cited as analogous contexts rather than HCC-specific evidence.

## Number and Basis of Main ICI Rechallenge Strategies in HCC

**Four main strategies** are described, defined by the combinations of agents used in the initial versus the rechallenge treatment [P1][P2].

### The four strategies [P2]

| # | Rechallenge regimen | Prior (initial) treatment | n (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Targeted therapy + anti-PD-L1 | Initial anti-PD-1 immunotherapy | 138 (36.0%) |
| 2 | Anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab + anti-PD-1 nivolumab | Initial targeted therapy + anti-PD-L1 | 100 (26.1%) |
| 3 | Anti-CTLA-4 tremelimumab + anti-PD-L1 durvalumab | Initial bevacizumab + atezolizumab | 132 (34.5%) |
| 4 | Targeted therapy + anti-PD-L1 after resistance to the *same* initial treatment | Same regimen (atezolizumab + bevacizumab) | 13 (3.4%) |

The classification is explicitly "according to the drug selection of initial ICI treatment and ICI rechallenge" [P2]. Of 383 patients across 12 clinical studies, 378 (98.7%) received combined regimens and only 5 (1.3%) a single agent (durvalumab, pembrolizumab, or ipilimumab) [P2].

### Basis and rationale

- **Empirical, not standardized:** No standardized rechallenge regimen, patient indications, or protocol exists; decisions are guided by empirical considerations including regional regulatory policy, drug availability, patient characteristics, and treatment-related factors [P1][P3].
- **Comparative performance:** Regimens 1 and 2 achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable outcomes than regimens 3 and 4; grade ≥3 irAEs ranged 15.0%–24.3% across all four, and combination strategies—particularly regimens 1 and 2—appeared to offer a better efficacy–safety balance [P2]. These comparisons are non-statistical, derived mainly from retrospective studies and case reports with substantial heterogeneity [P2].
- **Mechanistic rationale:** Renewed immune activation is attributed to immunogenic cell death, tumor microenvironment remodeling, and re-expression of inhibitory checkpoints such as PD-L1 or CTLA-4 [P1].

### Scope limitations and future directions

- **No local-therapy combinations yet:** For HCC there is currently no rechallenge regimen combining ICI with interventional therapy, radiotherapy, or other local treatments; a phase II trial is evaluating sintilimab plus stereotactic radiotherapy plus bevacizumab biosimilar IBI305 [P2].
- **Expansion proposed [P4]:** Future regimens should integrate immune modulation, targeted inhibition, and TME remodeling—e.g., novel ICIs (anti-TIGIT, anti-LAG3, PD-(L)1/CTLA-4 bispecifics), stroma modulators (galunisertib, SAR439459, bintrafusp alfa, FAP-targeted agents, navitoclax, PEGPH20, simtuzumab), and combinations with radiotherapy, TACE, TAI, or HAIC [P4].
- **Framing of the review [P3]:** The synthesis covers six dimensions—efficacy, safety, drug selection, rechallenge timing, patient-centered considerations, and molecular mechanisms—drawing on 10 retrospective studies, 2 prospective studies, and 11 case reports (383 patients, published 2021–2025) [P3]. Pooled data reflect no optimal indication or treatment strategy, so overall efficacy (ORR 13.8%, DCR 50.7%, mPFS 2.0–5.6 months) is lower than with initial ICI therapy [P3].
- **Supporting figures [F2]:** Fig. 2 presents the effectiveness data (BOR and mPFS for initial treatment vs. rechallenge; mOS for rechallenge) underlying the regimen comparisons [P6].
- **Safety context [P6]:** irAEs rose from 38.0% (initial) to 54.1% (rechallenge) and grade ≥3 irAEs from 8.0% to 19.5%, though fatal irAEs were fewer (0.3% vs. 3.1%); Table 1 tabulates the 12 studies by regimen category [P6].
- **Conclusion [P5]:** ICI rechallenge is "a rational and feasible therapeutic option for selected HCC patients," with future work needed on regimen selection, predictive biomarkers, and the molecular basis of immune reactivation [P5].

**Caveat:** The four-strategy taxonomy is the review authors' synthesis of heterogeneous, largely retrospective data; no head-to-head statistical comparison across regimens was performed [P2].

# Rechallenge Regimens with Relatively Better Outcomes Among the Four Strategies

## Direct answer

Among the four ICI rechallenge strategies, **regimen 1 (targeted therapy plus anti-PD-L1 following initial anti-PD-1 monotherapy)** and **regimen 2 (ipilimumab plus nivolumab after initial targeted and PD-L1 therapy)** achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable clinical outcomes than regimen 3 (tremelimumab plus durvalumab after bevacizumab and atezolizumab) and regimen 4 (rechallenge with the same bevacizumab plus atezolizumab regimen) [P1].

## Supporting outcome data (per regimen)

- **Regimen 1** (n = 138): ORR 17.4%, DCR 64.5%, mPFS 5.2–5.6 months; irAEs 60.9%, grade ≥3 irAEs 18.8% [P1].
- **Regimen 2** (n = 100): ORR 18.0%, DCR 45.0%, mPFS 2.4–3.0 months; irAEs 44.8%, grade ≥3 irAEs 16.4% [P1].
- **Regimen 3** (n = 132): ORR 6.8%, DCR 40.2%, mPFS 2.0–4.0 months; irAEs 51.4%, grade ≥3 irAEs 24.3% — described as "limited efficacy" with higher toxicity [P1].
- **Regimen 4** (n = 13): ORR 15.0%, DCR 54.0%, mPFS 4.7 months; irAEs 46.0%, grade ≥3 irAEs 15.0% — efficacy "appears modest" [P1].

Severe (grade ≥3) irAEs remained within 15.0%–24.3% across all four regimens, indicating an overall manageable safety profile [P1].

## Important caveats and limitations

- The review is **mainly based on retrospective studies and case reports**, with substantial interstudy heterogeneity; **no statistical comparisons were performed across regimens**, so findings should be interpreted with caution [P1].
- Four main strategies were defined by the combinations of agents used initially versus at rechallenge, most involving targeted therapy plus anti-PD-L1 or dual ICIs [P2].
- Patient selection modifies outcomes: preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI 1–2), age ≤60 years, and lower tumor burden are associated with more favorable outcomes; prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication but warrant close monitoring [P8].
- Future work should focus on optimizing regimen selection and predictive biomarkers to guide individualized rechallenge [P7], and on rationally designed combinations integrating immune modulation, targeted inhibition, and TME remodeling [P6].
- Rechallenge after pneumonitis is only recommended with complete resolution of grade 2 ICI-P, and safety of rechallenge after grade 3 toxicity has not been studied [P9].

## Note on evidence not relevant to this question

Several retrieved items do not address ICI rechallenge in HCC and therefore cannot inform the comparison: [P3] concerns self-management strategies for menstrual cycle symptoms; [P4] concerns PCNSL prognosis; [P5] concerns neonatal vancomycin dosing. No figure or table content ([F2] or otherwise) was available in the supplied evidence to corroborate the regimen-level ORR/DCR/mPFS values, which are cited here from the text of [P1] only.

# ORR for ICI Rechallenge vs. Initial ICI Therapy

## Pooled/aggregate comparison
In the reviewed HCC literature (10 retrospective studies, 2 prospective studies, 11 case reports; 383 patients with prior ICI exposure), the ORR of initial ICI treatment was **20.3%** [P1]. ICI rechallenge achieved a lower pooled ORR of **13.8%** [P1]. The review attributes this reduced efficacy to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge, both associated with ICI resistance, while cautioning that these are pooled data across heterogeneous studies without an optimal standardized rechallenge strategy [P1].

## Study-level comparisons (rechallenge higher than initial)
Several individual studies reported the opposite direction:
- Scheiner et al. [28]: ORR 26% with rechallenge vs. 22% with initial ICI therapy, including 11 PRs among 21 patients who had progressed on initial treatment [P1].
- Alden et al. [32]: ORR 22% with rechallenge vs. 6% with initial therapy, with 4 of 18 PD patients achieving objective response [P1].
- Wong et al. [31] and Roessler et al. [33] described patients with PD or SD on initial therapy who later achieved CR/PR on rechallenge [P1].

## Regimen-specific rechallenge ORRs
- Regimen 1 (targeted + anti-PD-L1 after anti-PD-1): ORR 17.4% [P3]
- Regimen 2 (ipilimumab + nivolumab): ORR 18.0% [P3]
- Regimen 3 (tremelimumab + durvalumab): ORR 6.8% [P3]
- Regimen 4 (same bevacizumab + atezolizumab): ORR 15.0% [P3]

## Figure-level data
The ORRs for initial therapy (20.3%) and rechallenge (13.8%) are presented graphically in **Fig. 2a and Fig. 2c**, respectively, with supporting data in online supplementary Tables 2 and 3 [P1]. Regimen-specific ORRs are also plotted in Fig. 2c [P3]. Note: the figure content itself is referenced but not reproduced in the evidence provided.

## Interpretation and limitations
The review's conclusion frames ICI rechallenge as "a rational and feasible therapeutic option for selected HCC patients, providing an opportunity to achieve additional clinical benefit after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation," while noting irAE frequency may increase but remains manageable [P5]. This conclusion is not a claim of superior ORR over initial therapy; rather, it reflects benefit in selected patients, consistent with the mixed direction of study-level findings [P1, P5].

**Important caveat — conflicting/heterogeneous evidence:** The pooled estimate (rechallenge 13.8% < initial 20.3%) [P1] conflicts with individual studies showing higher rechallenge ORR (26% vs. 22% [28]; 22% vs. 6% [32]) [P1]. These should not be merged: the pooled figure aggregates heterogeneous retrospective/prospective cohorts and case reports with no standardized regimen or indication, and no statistical comparison across studies was performed [P1, P3]. Population, dose, and subgroup conditions for the pooled comparison are **not stated** beyond the aggregate BCLC stage distribution and line-of-therapy breakdown [P1].

**Note on [P6]:** This passage concerns a post-marketing surveillance study of nivolumab in carcinoma of unknown primary (CUP), not ICI rechallenge in HCC. It reports that overall ORR was consistent with the NM-K2002 trial and that ORR was numerically higher in systemic treatment–naïve versus pretreated patients [P6]. It does **not** provide rechallenge-vs-initial ORR data for HCC and therefore cannot be used to answer the query; it is cited here only to document that it was reviewed and found non-contributory. Similarly, no relevant figure [F2] content on this comparison is available in the supplied evidence beyond the Fig. 2 references noted above [P1, P3].

**Bottom line:** The cited review reports a pooled rechallenge ORR of 13.8% versus 20.3% for initial ICI therapy [P1], but individual studies report higher rechallenge ORRs (up to 26% vs. 22%, and 22% vs. 6%) [P1]. These findings conflict and derive from heterogeneous, largely retrospective data without statistical cross-study comparison [P1, P3].

# Why Patient Selection Is Important for ICI Rechallenge in HCC

## 1. Core rationale: outcomes are driven by baseline characteristics and tumor biology

Patient selection is critical because clinical outcomes after ICI rechallenge are "profoundly influenced by baseline patient characteristics and tumor biology" [P3]. The review identifies selection as one of the unresolved priorities for future research, alongside regimen optimization, rechallenge timing, and response biomarkers [P1].

## 2. Documented prognostic factors supporting selection

- **Liver function**: Child-Pugh grade A and lower ALBI grades were associated with longer OS in two independent regimens; good liver function is "the most consistent prognostic predictor" across studies [P3].
- **Age and tumor burden**: Age ≤60 years and intrahepatic tumor number ≤10 were independent protective factors for OS [P3].
- **Inflammation**: NLR <3.1 was an independent protective factor for OS [P3].
- **Reason for discontinuation**: In HCC, nearly half of patients who stopped initial ICI for PD had BOR of PD at rechallenge, whereas all 5 who stopped for adverse events achieved disease control — though the small sample limits reliability [P2].
- **Progression pattern**: Existing lesions, new lesions, or vascular invasion may influence benefit [P2].
- **Safety**: Prior irAEs are "not an absolute contraindication" but warrant monitoring and individualized risk-benefit assessment [P3].

## 3. What remains uncertain (limits of selection criteria)

Prior BOR is controversial: some studies find prior response protective [P3], others find no association [P3]; an initial BOR of PD is "not a contraindication" [P3]. BMI, hepatitis virus infection status [P3], and PD-L1 expression, tertiary lymphoid structures, lymphocyte infiltration, microsatellite stability, and mutational load are largely uncharacterized for rechallenge in HCC [P3].

## 4. Methodological caveat

Rechallenge evidence derives primarily from retrospective cohorts "with significant selection bias and confounding by indication," and no validated risk stratification tool exists [P5]. This is itself a reason selection must be handled cautiously rather than algorithmically.

## 5. Required cross-referenced items

- **[P4]** In the ketogenic diet conclusion, the authors state that further mechanistic work and prospective trials are needed "to determine optimal patient selection, therapeutic combinations and long-term safety" [P4]. This is a general principle from a different intervention and does not provide HCC ICI-rechallenge-specific selection criteria; it is cited only as corroborating the broader call for prospective selection research.
- **[P8]** Argues that because the TME varies by genotype, treatment history, and resistance state, "patient selection should be based on prespecified biomarkers rather than on a generic diagnosis" [P8]. Candidate measures include immune-cell composition, CAF/ECM signatures, and hypoxia/metabolic profiles; however, these are explicitly "exploratory selection hypotheses rather than indications for clinical use" until prospectively validated [P8]. This is a cross-tumor principle, not HCC rechallenge data.
- **[P7]** In neutrophilic asthma, biologics "require careful patient selection based on inflammatory phenotype" [P7]. This is a different disease and drug class; it is cited only as an analogous precedent that phenotype-based selection governs biologic efficacy, not as HCC evidence.
- **[P9]** In melanoma, the magnitude of ICD induction is positively associated with anti-PD-1 responsiveness in the B16 model [P9]. This supports the general concept that response determinants can be measured and used for selection, but it is preclinical melanoma data and does not define HCC rechallenge selection criteria.
- **[P6]** For semaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide, side effects "can be minimized through individualized dose titration and careful patient selection" [P6]. This concerns incretin-based therapies, not ICIs, and is cited only as a general illustration of selection mitigating toxicity.
- **[P10]** Provides an example of operational selection in an HCC trial: inclusion requires BCLC B/C, ECOG 0–2, Child-Pugh A or B, and recurrence after curative-intent therapy; exclusion covers incomplete data, severe comorbidities, concurrent malignancies, and progression after non-curative therapy [P10]. This is a trial eligibility framework for TACE+TKI±PD-1, not a validated rechallenge selection rule.
- **[F2]** No figure or table with the ID F2 appears in the supplied evidence; therefore no claim can be attributed to it. This item cannot be discussed on the basis of the provided material.

## 6. Bottom line

Selection matters because the strongest and most reproducible outcome determinants in HCC rechallenge — liver function, tumor burden, age, NLR, and reason for discontinuation — are all baseline variables [P3][P2], while the biomarker-level determinants remain unvalidated [P3][P8]. Given that the underlying evidence is retrospective and confounded [P5], selection currently functions as an individualized risk-benefit judgment rather than a validated algorithm [P3][P5].

# Role of Liquid Biopsy with ctDNA in Advanced HCC

## 1. Rationale: compensating for the absence of routine tissue profiling
In HCC, tumor tissue biopsy is not mandatory for diagnosis, which complicates individualized precision medicine despite the availability of targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors [P2][P3]. Liquid biopsy — molecular profiling of ctDNA shed from tumors into circulation — is proposed as a noninvasive, safe alternative for cancer genomic profiling that could compensate for the lack of routine tissue-based genomic profiling in HCC [P2][P3].

## 2. Genomic concordance with tumor tissue (key evidence gap)
The clinical usefulness of ctDNA depends on how closely its genetic information reflects tumor tissue [P2]. However, few investigations have assessed concordance between next-generation sequencing (NGS) results from liquid biopsy and tumor tissue in HCC, and existing studies are constrained by limited sample numbers and a restricted target gene set, hampering such comparisons [P2]. One prospective cohort study (pretreatment plasma from 130 patients with advanced HCC undergoing tissue-based sequencing before systemic therapy, June 2020–October 2022) was designed to evaluate this concordance and feasibility in patients treated with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (atezo/bev), the first-line standard of care [P3]. **The evidence provided does not report the concordance results of that study.**

## 3. Prognostic and monitoring role (investigational)
- ctDNA offers a minimally invasive approach for assessing tumor-derived molecular signals and potential minimal residual disease (MRD) [P7].
- Postoperative ctDNA positivity is associated with increased recurrence risk after curative-intent treatment, per recent meta-analytic evidence; however, reported sensitivity varies substantially across studies due to differences in assay design, tumor shedding, and analytical methods [P7].
- Accordingly, ctDNA is characterized as **a promising investigational biomarker for recurrence-risk stratification and MRD assessment, rather than a validated basis for altering surgery or adjuvant treatment in routine HCC practice** [P7]. Its clinical role remains primarily prognostic, investigational, or hypothesis-generating, and integration into treatment decisions requires prospective validation that biomarker-guided interventions improve clinically meaningful outcomes [P7].

## 4. Broader cfDNA context in HCC
cfDNA is the most widely studied liquid biopsy marker across several cancers, including liver cancer; the liver's abundant blood supply and tumor-related hepatocyte necrosis drive abundant tumor-derived cfDNA into peripheral blood, making HCC well suited to cfDNA detection [P1]. Three mainstream cfDNA detection modalities are mutation analysis, tissue-specific methylation profiling, and fragmentomics [P1]. Prior studies confirm cfDNA's diagnostic value for HCC, though marked interstudy heterogeneity persists [P1].

## Limitations of the evidence
- The concordance/feasibility findings of the atezo/bev cohort [P3] are not reported in the supplied text.
- No evidence in the provided passages establishes a validated predictive or treatment-guiding role for ctDNA in advanced HCC; the cited characterization is explicitly investigational/prognostic [P7].
- Several retrieved passages concern other tumor types (breast cancer [P4], colorectal cancer [P8][P9]) or other analytes/technologies (circulating RNA [P5], nanoparticles [P6], exosomes [P10]) and do not directly address ctDNA in advanced HCC.

# Limits on Precision Medicine in HCC According to the ctDNA Paper

## 1. Core limitation stated by the ctDNA paper: absence of mandatory tissue biopsy

The ctDNA study frames the central barrier explicitly: precision medicine in HCC is hindered by the lack of mandatory tissue biopsy for genomic profiling. The abstract states that "precision medicine is hindered by the lack of mandatory tissue biopsy for genomic profiling in HCC" [P4]. The Introduction elaborates that although targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors have raised the importance of individualized precision medicine based on tumor characteristics, "tumor tissue biopsy is not required for HCC diagnosis, making precision medicine more challenging" [P3]. Liquid biopsy (ctDNA) is proposed to compensate for this gap, but the paper notes that few studies have assessed ctDNA–tissue concordance in HCC, and existing studies are constrained by limited sample numbers and restricted target gene sets [P3].

## 2. Limited therapeutic utility because HCC lacks established druggable targets

The Discussion states directly: "because HCC lacks established druggable targets, the therapeutic utility of ctDNA remains limited, and prognostic biomarkers, like maxVAF, must be further validated in larger, independent cohorts as predictive tools" [P6]. Thus even where ctDNA profiling is feasible, its actionability is constrained, and maxVAF remains prognostic rather than established as predictive [P6].

## 3. Technical and biological limits of ctDNA measurement

The paper reports several assay-level constraints: TERT promoter mutations were less frequent than in the GENIE cohort, possibly reflecting the cohort's HBV-related etiology (viral integration not assessable by promoter-hotspot panels) and the high GC content of the TERT promoter complicating sequencing [P6]. Concordance was affected by sampling interval (sensitivity improved to 96.3% when restricted to ≤30 days) and by tissue type (high sensitivity/low PPV in biopsies vs. low sensitivity/high PPV in surgical specimens) [P6]. CNVs showed low concordance, attributed to low CNV frequency and inherent technical/biological limitations of ctDNA for CNVs or gene fusions, and clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential could not be entirely excluded [P6]. General limitations included a single East Asian, HBV-endemic cohort requiring external validation, and only single pretreatment blood samples [P6].

## 4. Related evidence on ctDNA as investigational only

A separate review passage likewise concludes that "ctDNA currently represents a promising investigational biomarker for recurrence-risk stratification and MRD assessment, rather than a validated basis for altering surgery or adjuvant treatment in routine HCC practice," with sensitivity varying substantially across studies due to assay design, tumor shedding, and analytical methods [P7].

## 5. Broader precision-medicine barriers in HCC from other evidence

- **Tumor heterogeneity and cell plasticity:** HCC is described as "a highly heterogeneous tumor with high cellular diversity, a key factor in therapeutic failures," with TFEB-driven hepatocyte-to-BEC-like transdifferentiation contributing to malignancy and poor outcomes; identifying this subset for precision medicine is proposed as a future strategy rather than an established one [P8].
- **Biomarker gaps for immunotherapy:** In the immuno-oncology context, "the absence of reliable biomarkers to anticipate primary resistance, detect emerging secondary resistance, or guide rational sequencing and combination strategies further limits the precision of immunotherapy," and validated predictive tools integrating benefit and toxicity risk are lacking [P2].
- **Exosome-based approaches:** Exosomal miRNAs show context-dependent, non-uniform effects depending on donor cell, recipient cell, and disease context, and external validation plus standardized analytical pipelines remain necessary before clinical translation [P5].

## 6. Items without relevant HCC precision-medicine content

The remaining required items do not address HCC precision medicine and therefore cannot be used to answer this question: [P1] concerns methodological caveats of feline oral microbiome diagnostics (selection bias, non-standardized phenotyping, single-time-point sampling); [P9] concerns antibiotic therapy for neutrophilic asthma; and [F2] is not present in the supplied evidence. No claim about HCC precision medicine is drawn from these sources.

**Summary:** According to the ctDNA paper, precision medicine in HCC is limited chiefly by the non-mandatory nature of tissue biopsy for genomic profiling [P3][P4], the absence of established druggable targets that restricts ctDNA's therapeutic utility [P6], and technical/biological constraints on ctDNA concordance and predictive validation [P6], with complementary barriers of tumor heterogeneity [P8] and biomarker gaps [P2][P5][P7].

# EV Cargo and Its Importance in Breast Cancer

## 1. What cargo do EVs carry?

**General cargo classes.** EVs are membrane-bound, lipid-bilayered particles secreted by diverse cell types that carry **proteins, lipids, DNA, and RNA**, and they mediate intercellular communication by transporting bioactive cargo between cells [P2]. EVs "reflect the molecular composition of their cell of origin" and are abundant in human body fluids [P2]. A parallel statement describes EVs as transporting "bioactive molecules such as proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, including miRNAs" [P7], and another source lists "nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids" [P3].

**RNA cargo in breast cancer specifically.**
- EVs **protect their RNA cargo from degradation** in the extracellular environment and transfer RNAs between cells [P10].
- **miRNAs** (18–24 nt, non-coding) bind target mRNAs to suppress translation [P10].
- **lncRNAs** (>200 nt) regulate gene expression by "sponging" miRNAs (ceRNA mechanism) [P10].
- **circRNAs** (covalently closed loops lacking 5′ caps/3′ poly(A) tails) are highly stable, resistant to exonuclease degradation, and "often enriched in extracellular vesicles including exosomes and microvesicles" [P10].
- Together these form "a coordinated network that can be transferred to recipient cells to reprogramme post-transcriptional gene expression and facilitate pro-metastatic signalling" [P10].

**Protein cargo in breast cancer.** Proteomic analysis of sEVs from BC cell lines identified metastasis-associated proteins including **Ezrin, annexin A5, annexin A6, tenascin, and EMMPRIN/CD147** [P10]. lEVs are reported to transport "surface antigens, oncogenic products, and adhesion molecules on their surface or within vesicles" [P2].

**Immune-related cargo (tumor EVs, including breast cancer contexts).** Tumor exosomes can display **PD-L1** and inhibit cytotoxic T cells [P1]. In breast cancer, Munc13-4 was identified as a trafficking regulator promoting PD-L1 sorting and secretion via exosomes; its genetic deletion enhanced T cell–mediated antitumor immunity, suppressed tumor growth, and improved immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy [P8]. PD-L1⁺ tumor-derived EVs can act as antibody "decoys," being phagocytosed and degraded by macrophages, thereby mediating resistance to anti–PD-L1 therapy [P8]. Immunocyte-derived sEVs carrying **PD-1 and CD80** induced adaptive redistribution of PD-L1 in tumor cells and downregulated adhesion/antigen-presentation molecules, converting tumors to an immunologically cold phenotype [P8]. Separately, exosomes bearing **MHC class I-restricted tumor antigens** can activate T cells and provoke antitumor immune responses [P1].

## 2. Why is this important in breast cancer?

**Intercellular communication and metastatic progression.** EVs are "a key mediator of intercellular communication," with lEVs and sEVs delivering bioactive cargo associated with cancer-related processes (progression, metastasis, angiogenesis) [P2]. The pro-metastatic functions of EVs "are driven by their diverse cargo, which includes proteins and nucleic acids"; these molecules are internalised by recipient cells, modify the recipient phenotype, and modulate the metastatic cascade [P10]. Distinct EV subpopulations contribute to the tumour microenvironment, premetastatic niche formation, immune evasion, extracellular matrix remodelling, and BC organotropism [P5].

**Clinical stakes.** Approximately 20–30% of early-stage BC patients develop distant metastases within 10 years, and metastasis accounts for nearly 90% of BC-related deaths [P2].

**Biomarker and therapeutic relevance.** EVs are highlighted as potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers and viable therapeutic targets in BC [P5]; they offer "a biologically attractive biomarker model because they carry a multimolecular payload reflecting cellular status and intercellular communication" [P9]. In TNBC, BCSC-derived exosomes enriched in lnc-PDGFD activate lung fibroblasts via YBX1/NF-κB, and fibroblast-secreted IL-11 promotes lung metastasis; knocking out lnc-PDGFD in BCSC exosomes markedly reduced lung metastasis in vivo [P8].

## 3. Caveats and limitations stated in the evidence

- **Evidence grading:** The BC review assigns each RNA and protein cargo a graded evidence level, noting this is the first review to apply such grading systematically to EV cargoes in BC metastasis [P2].
- **Heterogeneity/translation barriers:** EV size ranges overlap, isolation methods can recover non-vesicular particles (exomeres, supermeres), and sEV/lEV are not used interchangeably with exosome/microvesicle [P2]; EV heterogeneity and molecular complexity are considerable barriers to clinical translation [P5].
- **Conflicting/context-dependent framing (not merged):** Tumor-derived EVs are described as having a "dualistic influence"—immunosuppressive (PD-L1⁺ exosomes inhibiting cytotoxic T cells) versus immunostimulatory (MHC class I-restricted antigen-bearing exosomes activating T cells), and are "context-dependent" [P1]. The specific conditions (population, dose, subgroup) determining which phenotype predominates are **not stated** in [P1].
- **Non-BC evidence:** Several cargo/function statements come from non-breast contexts—e.g., EBV-derived exosomes carrying LMP1, LMP2A, EBERs, and BART miRNAs [P3][P6], and CRC/HCC EV examples (lncRNA WEE2-AS1, miR-135a-5p, ADAM17) [P8]. These should not be generalized to breast cancer without qualification.

# Global Challenges in Colorectal Cancer Burden Despite Screening

## 1. Persistent absolute burden despite screening gains
Population-based screening has reduced CRC incidence and mortality in many older adults, yet the absolute global burden remains high due to demographic aging, unequal access to care, and persistent exposure to modifiable risks [P5]. CRC remains the second leading cause of cancer-related death globally, a persistent clinical burden despite advances in screening and treatment [P2]. Worldwide figures cited include more than 1.9 million new cases and over 900,000 deaths in 2022 [P1], and approximately 2 million new cases and over 900,000 deaths annually [P4].

## 2. Rising early-onset CRC
Although screening has reduced incidence and mortality in older adults, the increasing burden of early-onset CRC underscores the need for more effective prevention, detection, and treatment strategies [P2]. Early-onset CRC has emerged as a major challenge, with the relative contribution and causal importance of life-course environmental, metabolic, inflammatory, and microbial exposures remaining incompletely defined [P5].

## 3. Inequitable screening coverage and access
Screening coverage varies widely across regions, with high uptake in some high-income countries and persistently low participation in many low- and middle-income settings; even within countries, disparities across socioeconomic and demographic groups exacerbate inequalities in disease burden [P6]. CRC epidemiology shows a paradoxical pattern of declining rates in screened populations but an increasing global burden, particularly among younger individuals and in transitioning economies, reflecting demographic change, lifestyle transitions, and unequal access to healthcare [P10].

## 4. Limited performance of newer screening modalities
Blood-based testing does not outperform colonoscopy or FIT; its role is participation-enhancing rather than a preventive equivalent, particularly given limited sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions (13.2% for advanced precancerous lesions vs. 83.1% for CRC in ECLIPSE) [P9]. Long-term effects on interval cancer and mortality remain under evaluation [P9].

## 5. Treatment-refractory disease and therapeutic gaps
Metastatic CRC continues to be associated with poor long-term outcomes, particularly in patients who do not benefit from ICIs [P1]. Challenges include a relatively low early diagnosis rate, drug resistance, and the limited proportion of patients responding to immunotherapy [P4]. MSS/pMMR tumors predominate and remain largely refractory to ICI monotherapy, with response rates generally below 10% [P1, P8].

## 6. Biological and host-factor complexity
Epidemiological patterns are closely linked to underlying biological mechanisms, including metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and microbiota alterations [P10]. Systemic inflammation and immunosuppression coexist in patients with CRC—reduced CD8+ T cells, expanded IL-10+ macrophages, and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles (e.g., propionate negatively correlated with IL-6 and IL-13)—suggesting immunometabolic dysregulation as an additional layer of disease burden [P7].

## The Central Paradox of Immune Checkpoint Blockade (ICI Position Article)

### The paradox as stated in the position article

The ICI position article explicitly frames the central paradox of immune checkpoint blockade as follows: **the same immune activation that can generate durable tumor control may also produce clinically meaningful toxicity, whereas in other patients, it fails to elicit sufficient antitumor activity** [P1]. The article situates this paradox within its broader argument that the field has moved "from promise to plateau," and that understanding this plateau requires examining immune-related adverse events, primary and acquired resistance, biomarker limitations, and special populations [P1].

### Supporting and contextual evidence

- **Heterogeneous responses and resistance** are consistent with the "failure to elicit sufficient antitumor activity" arm of the paradox: although ICB targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 has transformed treatment of multiple malignancies by restoring T-cell effector function, "clinical responses remain heterogeneous, and resistance frequently emerges" [P2].
- **Toxicity as the other arm of the paradox** is reflected in the literature on immune-related adverse events, which the position article identifies as a major clinical barrier [P1]; related reviews likewise emphasize irAE recognition as an increasingly important clinical competency as ICIs enter earlier and broader treatment settings [A5][A7].

- **A related but distinct "paradox" in MSS CRC** is described as immune presence without immune competence — checkpoint blockade "often releases the brake on an immune system that lacks metabolic capacity" [P6]. Again, this is a resistance-framing paradox, not the position article's central paradox.

# Comparison of Efficacy vs. Safety Evidence for ICI Rechallenge in HCC

## 1. Nature and strength of the evidence base

Both efficacy and safety rest on the same body of literature: 10 retrospective studies, 2 prospective studies, and 11 case reports, collectively covering 383 HCC patients with prior ICI exposure [P8]. The review itself characterizes the overall evidence as "variable but notable antitumor activity with an acceptable safety profile" [P7], and states that "ICI rechallenge has shown both efficacy and acceptable safety in certain HCC patients" while many clinical and scientific questions remain unresolved [P2]. Critically, the authors caution that the review is "mainly based on retrospective studies and case reports," with substantial heterogeneity and no statistical comparisons across regimens [P3].

## 2. Efficacy evidence

**Pooled outcomes:** Rechallenge achieved ORR 13.8%, DCR 50.7%, mPFS 2.0–5.6 months, and median OS 7.4–16.7 months — all lower than the initial ICI treatment (ORR 20.3%, DCR 69.0%, mPFS 3.7–5.4 months) [P8]. The authors attribute this to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge, but caution that these are pooled data without an optimized indication or treatment strategy [P8].

**Regimen-specific efficacy** (Table 1; Fig. 2c–e) [P3]:
- Regimen 1 (targeted + anti-PD-L1 after anti-PD-1): ORR 17.4%, DCR 64.5%, mPFS 5.2–5.6 months
- Regimen 2 (ipilimumab + nivolumab): ORR 18.0%, DCR 45.0%, mPFS 2.4–3.0 months
- Regimen 3 (tremelimumab + durvalumab): ORR 6.8%, DCR 40.2%, mPFS 2.0–4.0 months
- Regimen 4 (same atezolizumab + bevacizumab): ORR 15.0%, DCR 54.0%, mPFS 4.7 months

Regimens 1 and 2 achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable outcomes [P3].

**Comparative efficacy vs. TKI:** No head-to-head study exists in HCC [P1]. An international multicenter retrospective study reported median post-progression survival of 14.9 vs. 8.4 months for rechallenge vs. TKI monotherapy, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.25) [P1]. The phase III CONTACT-03 trial in renal cell carcinoma found rechallenge was not better than TKI monotherapy [P1].

**Predictors of efficacy:** Preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI 1–2), age ≤60 years, lower tumor burden, and NLR <3.1 [P9]. The association between initial BOR and rechallenge outcome remains controversial across studies [P9]. The authors speculate that efficacy may differ between patients discontinuing due to progression versus adverse events — Miura et al. reported all 5 patients discontinuing for AEs achieved SD, whereas nearly half of 11 discontinuing for PD had PD at rechallenge, though the small sample limits reliability [P6].

## 3. Safety evidence

**Pooled irAE rates:** irAEs rose from 38.0% (initial) to 54.1% (rechallenge); grade ≥3 irAEs from 8.0% to 19.5% [P5]. This increase aligns with observations in other malignancies and may relate to prolonged/repeated ICI administration [P5].

**Regimen-specific safety** (Fig. 3c, d) [P3]:
- Regimen 1: irAEs 60.9%, grade ≥3 18.8%
- Regimen 2: irAEs 44.8%, grade ≥3 16.4%
- Regimen 3: irAEs 51.4%, grade ≥3 24.3% (highest toxicity; requires careful selection and monitoring)
- Regimen 4: irAEs 46.0%, grade ≥3 15.0%

Across all four regimens, grade ≥3 irAEs remained within 15.0%–24.3%, indicating an overall manageable safety profile [P3].

**Fatal irAEs:** Only 1 (0.3%) fatal irAE across 12 clinical studies and 11 case reports — lower than 3.1% following initial ICI treatment [P5]. Most irAEs were controllable with ICI discontinuation, corticosteroids, and other approaches [P5].

**Timing and safety:** Safety did not differ significantly between intervals of <1 month vs. >1 month (grade ≥3 irAEs 11.4% vs. 14.7%) [P4].

**Prior irAE history:** Among 7 patients (22%) with prior irAEs, 3 developed recurrent irAEs during dual-ICI rechallenge, mostly manageable with corticosteroids allowing treatment continuation; prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication [P9].

## 4. Key asymmetries and caveats in the two evidence streams

1. **Direction of change:** Efficacy is *lower* at rechallenge than at initial treatment (ORR 13.8% vs. 20.3%) [P8], whereas irAE frequency is *higher* (54.1% vs. 38.0%; grade ≥3 19.5% vs. 8.0%) [P5] — though fatal irAEs are paradoxically fewer (0.3% vs. 3.1%) [P5].

2. **Confounding by selection bias — explicitly flagged for safety:** Patients who experienced severe irAEs tended not to be readministered, suggesting the study population may be enriched for tolerators; results may also be influenced by shorter follow-up and smaller cohorts [P5]. This caveat is stated for safety but not equivalently quantified for efficacy.

3. **Conflicting/heterogeneous efficacy signals:** Some individual studies report *higher* ORR at rechallenge than initial therapy (Scheiner 26% vs. 22%; Alden 22% vs. 6%) [P8], which conflicts with the pooled lower efficacy — the authors note no optimal strategy was applied across studies [P8]. No corresponding conflict is reported for safety, where the direction (increased irAEs) is consistent [P5].

4. **Comparative evidence gap:** For efficacy, the only comparison against TKI is retrospective and non-significant (p = 0.25), with CONTACT-03 (RCC) negative [P1]. For safety, no head-to-head comparison against TKIs is reported at all in the provided evidence — not stated [P1].

5. **Biomarker maturity:** Predictive biomarkers for both benefit and toxicity remain exploratory in HCC; lymphatic/tertiary lymphoid structure and ctDNA data are extrapolated from melanoma/lung cancer, and autoimmune/HLA predictors of severe irAEs derive from melanoma and RCC cohorts, not HCC [P1].

## 5. Bottom line

Efficacy evidence is quantitatively richer (regimen-level ORR/DCR/mPFS/OS, comparative PPS data vs. TKI) but internally inconsistent and uniformly non-randomized [P1][P3][P8]. Safety evidence is more directionally consistent (uniformly increased irAEs, uniformly manageable grade ≥3 rates, low fatal irAE rate) but is explicitly acknowledged to be confounded by selection bias and short follow-up [P5]. The review's own conclusion — that combination strategies, particularly regimens 1 and 2, offer "a more favorable balance between efficacy and safety" — is offered with the caveat that findings derive mainly from retrospective studies and require confirmation in well-designed prospective trials [P3], a need reiterated in the future-directions section [P2].

**Short answer: No — the evidence supports benefit only in *selected* HCC patients, and the strength of that conclusion is limited by the nature and quality of the available data.**

## 1. Benefit is restricted to selected patients, not all

- ICI rechallenge is described as "a rational and feasible therapeutic option for **selected** HCC patients, providing an opportunity to achieve additional clinical benefit after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation" [P1]; the same framing is repeated in the Key Messages [P2].
- Across published studies, rechallenge showed "**variable** but notable antitumor activity with an acceptable safety profile" [P2] — i.e., responses are heterogeneous rather than universal.
- Clinical benefit "appears to be more frequently observed" in patients with preserved liver function, age <60 years, and lower tumor burden [P2]. Consistently, good liver function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI grades 1–2), younger age (≤60 years), and lower tumor burden "may be associated with more favorable outcomes" [P5]. Good liver function is described as "the most consistent prognostic predictor" across studies [P5].
- Additional candidate selection factors: NLR <3.1 as an independent protective factor for OS [P5]; intrahepatic tumor number ≤10 and age ≤60 years as independent protective factors [P5].
- Prior irAEs are "not an absolute contraindication" but warrant close monitoring and individualized risk–benefit assessment [P5]; the frequency of irAEs may increase with rechallenge, though most remain manageable [P1][P2].

## 2. What limits the conclusion

**(a) No standardized regimen or patient indications.** There is "no standardized rechallenge regimen, patient indications, and few studies on its mechanism" [P2]. Four main strategies have been described, most involving targeted therapy plus anti-PD-L1 or dual ICIs [P2]; in the reviewed studies, 378/383 patients (98.7%) received combination regimens and only 5 (1.3%) a single agent [S3].

**(b) Heterogeneity and selection bias.** The favourable-characteristic findings "require cautious interpretation due to interstudy heterogeneity and potential selection bias" [P2].

**(c) Small samples in key supporting studies.** In Miura et al., "the small sample size in that study limited the reliability of these findings" [P6].

**(d) Unresolved questions remain.** "Many clinical and scientific questions remain unresolved" despite demonstrated efficacy and acceptable safety in certain patients [P4].

**(e) No consensus on timing.** "There remains no definitive conclusion regarding when ICI rechallenge should be initiated after the end of initial ICI treatment" [P7]; no study reports direct rechallenge without an interval [P7], and there is no consensus on interval treatment [P7].

**(f) Predictive biomarkers are unestablished in HCC.** PD-L1 expression, tertiary lymphoid structures, lymphocyte infiltration, microsatellite stability and mutational load influence *initial* ICI efficacy, but "little is known about their effects on ICI rechallenge in HCC patients" [P5]; the predictive value of lymphatic vessels/tertiary lymphoid structures for rechallenge "remains unclear" [P8].

**(g) Conflicting evidence on prior response as a predictor.** Lai et al. reported prior response to initial anti-PD-1 as an independent protective factor for OS (but not PFS) [P5]; Cho et al. reported all patients with PD as initial BOR also had PD at rechallenge (3/3), whereas those with SD achieved 60% DCR (9/15) [P5]; **in contrast**, Wong et al. found neither primary nor acquired resistance associated with OS after rechallenge [P5]. The review's own resolution is limited: "the only thing we can be certain of is that an initial BOR of PD is not a contraindication" [P5]. Limiting conditions: these derive from different regimens (regimen 1 vs 2 vs 3) and retrospective designs; population/dose details are not stated in the provided passages.

**(h) No randomized head-to-head data versus TKIs.** "There is no study on strictly 'head-to-head' comparing the efficacy and safety of ICI rechallenge versus TKIs," most data are retrospective or real-world, and high-quality RCTs are lacking [P8]. An international retrospective study showed median post-progression survival of 14.9 vs 8.4 months (rechallenge vs TKI) but the difference was **not statistically significant (p = 0.25)** [P8]; moreover, the phase III CONTACT-03 trial in renal cell carcinoma found rechallenge after immunotherapy failure was not better than TKI monotherapy [P8] — a cross-tumour caution, not HCC-specific.

**(i) Mechanistic uncertainty for some strategies.** The effectiveness of anti-CTLA-4 rechallenge alone in patients who received prior anti-PD-1/PD-L1 "has not been reported," and simple switching "may not fully overcome these resistance mechanisms" [P3].

## 3. Note on scope
The retrieved evidence on rechallenge comes from a single narrative review [P1–P8]; no primary comparative trial data in HCC are included. One passage [P9] concerns ocular irAE rechallenge management (rechallenge considered only after complete resolution and multidisciplinary risk–benefit discussion, generally avoided after grade 4 toxicity) but is not HCC-rechallenge-specific evidence and is cited here only as a safety caveat.

# Why an Initial Response to ICI Does Not Guarantee Continued Benefit in HCC

## Direct HCC evidence

The most directly relevant evidence comes from the ICI rechallenge literature in HCC [P2]. This review reports that the association between the best overall response (BOR) to initial ICI treatment and outcomes after rechallenge "remains controversial" [P2]. Specifically:

- Lai et al. [29] found that a prior response to initial anti-PD-1 treatment was an independent protective factor for overall survival (OS), **but not** for progression-free survival (PFS), in HCC patients following ICI rechallenge [P2].
- Cho et al. [37] reported that patients with progressive disease (PD) as their initial BOR all showed PD again during rechallenge (n = 3/3), whereas those with stable disease (SD) as initial BOR achieved a disease control rate of 60% (n = 9/15) [P2].
- In contrast, Wong et al. [31] reported that **neither** primary nor acquired resistance to initial ICI treatment was associated with OS after rechallenge [P2].
- Across regimens 1, 2, and 4, some patients who had PD as their initial BOR still responded to ICI rechallenge [P2].
- Roessler et al. [33] found that a short duration of disease control with initial ICI treatment did not necessarily preclude benefit from rechallenge [P2].

Thus, the review concludes only that "an initial BOR of PD is not a contraindication for ICI rechallenge" [P2]. Notably, the evidence does not provide a mechanistic explanation specific to HCC for why initial response fails to translate into durable benefit; the review states that little is known about the effects of PD-L1 expression, tertiary lymphoid structures, lymphocyte infiltration, microsatellite stability, and mutational load on ICI rechallenge in HCC, although these are considered to influence initial ICI effectiveness [P2].

## Mechanistic explanations from other tumor types (not HCC-specific)

The evidence base contains mechanistic discussions of adaptive/acquired resistance, but these are drawn from **melanoma** and **esophageal carcinoma**, not HCC:

- In melanoma, adaptive resistance is described as a reversible, treatment-induced response dependent on sustained therapeutic pressure; compensatory IFN-γ signaling induces transcriptional upregulation of PD-L1 via JAK-STAT, establishing a negative feedback loop that facilitates immune evasion. This "provides a mechanistic explanation for the clinical pattern of an initial response followed by later disease progression in patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy" [P3]. Acquired resistance (e.g., JAK1/JAK2 alterations) represents the predominant mechanism underlying late-stage relapse [P3].
- In esophageal carcinoma, "primary resistance affects over 60% of patients, while others develop acquired resistance after initial response," and ICI efficacy is constrained by "both incomplete initial sensitivity and adaptive escape during therapy" [P4].
- More broadly, many patients show primary resistance and others later develop acquired resistance after an initial response, suggesting checkpoint signaling alone does not fully explain long-term immune failure; metabolic stress and loss of mitochondrial fitness in TILs limit the durability of responses to PD-1 blockade [P5].

**Limiting condition:** These mechanisms are established in melanoma [P3], esophageal carcinoma [P4], and general oncology [P5]; the evidence does not state that they have been validated in HCC.

## Additional contextual factors (not direct explanations)

- The gut microbiome has been associated with ICI outcomes in melanoma, NSCLC, and HCC, but taxa are inconsistent across studies and no universally favorable signature is defined [P8].
- In ICI-related colitis, a subset of patients (~10%) with initial symptom remission may develop recurrent symptoms, particularly upon resuming immunotherapy, especially anti-CTLA-4 agents [P6]; this concerns toxicity recurrence, not antitumor response.
- In AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma, relapse is defined as new lesions after initial response and treatment termination [P7] — a definitional framework, not HCC evidence.
- The mucosal epithelium orchestrates the initial immune response to HPV [P9] — unrelated to ICI response durability.
- In IBD, secondary loss of response affects up to 45% of initial responders to any given agent [P1] — an analogous pattern in a non-oncologic disease, not HCC.
- Identifying mechanistically plausible targets does not guarantee clinical benefit; biological associations require validation [P10].
- No figure or table [F2] content was provided in the evidence; therefore no figure/table-based evidence can be cited for this question.

## Summary

The evidence directly addressing HCC [P2] shows that the relationship between initial ICI response and subsequent benefit is **controversial and inconsistent across studies**: prior response predicted OS but not PFS in one analysis [P2], was not associated with OS in another [P2], and some initial non-responders still benefited from rechallenge [P2]. Mechanistic explanations for response followed by progression (adaptive IFN-γ/JAK-STAT-driven PD-L1 upregulation, acquired JAK alterations) are documented in melanoma [P3] and esophageal carcinoma [P4], but **the evidence does not establish these mechanisms in HCC**. A definitive HCC-specific mechanistic answer is therefore **not available** in the provided literature.

## EV Heterogeneity as a Barrier to Clinical Translation in Breast Cancer

### Direct evidence from the breast cancer review

**1. Heterogeneity and molecular complexity are named as barriers per se.**
The BC-focused review states that "the full scope of EV function in BC metastasis remains unclear, and their inherent heterogeneity and molecular complexity present considerable barriers to clinical translation" [P6]. It further argues that addressing these challenges requires "a clear understanding of the distinct functions of each EV subpopulation" plus advanced single-EV analysis [P6].

**2. The experimental–clinical gap is attributed partly to intrinsic EV heterogeneity.**
The same review notes that the Phase I success rate for oncology drug development is only ~3.4%, and that "the gap between experimental findings and real-world outcomes partly stems from the difficulty in replicating the complexity of cancer biology in current functional studies and partly from the intrinsic heterogeneity of EV populations" [P7]. The proposed remedy is single-EV analysis (nano-flow cytometry, droplet-based assays, Raman spectrometry, aptamer-based detection, single-EV imaging) to "resolve vesicle heterogeneity" and identify metastasis-specific subpopulations "that may be obscured in conventional bulk EV studies" [P7].

**3. The mechanistic basis of the heterogeneity (as described in BC).**
BC EVs comprise distinct subpopulations—sEVs (~50–200 nm), lEVs (~150–500 nm), and apoptotic bodies (~500–4000 nm)—with distinct roles in progression and metastasis [P7]. The review explicitly notes that size ranges overlap and that common isolation methods also recover non-vesicular particles (exomeres, supermeres), so sEV/lEV are used as size-based categories rather than origin indicators [P7]. This is the mechanistic reason why bulk EV measurements cannot assign a function to a defined vesicle type.

### Supporting evidence from other cancer contexts (not breast cancer)

- In cancer-associated cachexia, "the marked heterogeneity of EV profiles and cytokine signatures across different tumor types poses a significant barrier to their broad applicability" [P1]; heterogeneous EV origins from multiple cell types "complicate the identification of tumor-specific signals" [P2].
- In the CAC context, EV heterogeneity is listed alongside incomplete understanding of selective cargo loading, limited tissue-specific targeting, off-target effects, and absent standardized manufacturing/QC as factors that "continue to restrict clinical development" [P5].

### Important scope limitations

- **No breast-cancer-specific quantitative data** on the magnitude of EV heterogeneity, its effect size on assay performance, or its impact on any named clinical trial are provided in the evidence. The BC claims are framed as review-level assertions [P6, P7]; the specific conditions (subtype, stage, EV isolation method, cohort) under which heterogeneity impairs translation are **not stated**.
- **Heterogeneity is not isolated as a single causal variable.** In the BC review it is presented jointly with "molecular complexity" [P6] and with the general difficulty of replicating cancer biology [P7]; in the CAC review it is bundled with cargo-loading, targeting, off-target, and manufacturing gaps [P5]. No source disentangles the relative contribution of EV heterogeneity from these co-listed barriers.
- **Sources from other disease areas** (osteoarthritis [P4, P8], bacterial EVs [P3], hyperforin [P9], phage therapy [P10]) describe analogous variability barriers (source/isolation/purification/characterization [P4]; strain-, dose-, and purity-dependent cargo [P3]) but are **not** breast cancer evidence and should not be generalized to BC.
- Related abstracts [A1]–[A10] concern tumour, immune, and genomic heterogeneity in BC but **do not address EV heterogeneity**; they cannot be used to support this answer.

### Bottom line (evidence-supported)

In BC, EV heterogeneity is described as a barrier because (i) functionally distinct vesicle subpopulations coexist and are not resolvable by conventional bulk methods, with overlapping sizes and co-isolated non-vesicular particles [P7]; and (ii) this obscures which vesicle population carries a given metastatic function, contributing to the mismatch between experimental findings and clinical outcomes [P6, P7]. The evidence does not quantify this barrier or specify the conditions under which it operates.

# Screening and Colorectal Cancer Incidence: Documented Effects and Unresolved Questions

## 1. Documented reductions in incidence and mortality

Population-based screening has been credited with measurable reductions in CRC incidence and mortality. Countries with well-established, population-based screening programs "have achieved substantial reductions in CRC incidence and mortality" [P2]. Similarly, screening "has reduced incidence and mortality in older adults" [P1], and "population-based screening has reduced incidence and mortality in many older adults" [P9].

## 2. Why the absolute burden persists despite screening

The incidence reduction is bounded by countervailing forces. Although screening has lowered incidence in older adults, "the absolute global burden remains high because of demographic aging, unequal access to care, and persistent exposure to modifiable risks" [P9]. Screening coverage varies widely: uptake is high in some high-income countries but persistently low in many low- and middle-income settings, and within-country disparities across socioeconomic and demographic groups "further exacerbate inequalities in disease burden" [P2]. The rising burden of early-onset CRC also "underscores the need for more effective prevention, detection, and treatment strategies" [P1].

## 3. Unresolved issues

**(a) Equity and participation.** The evidence stresses that implementing programs is insufficient; "ensuring equitable access and adherence" remains an open challenge [P2].

**(b) Blood-based screening's downstream effects.** Positive blood tests "still require diagnostic colonoscopy, and long-term effects on interval cancer and mortality remain under evaluation" [P6]. Blood-based testing is positioned as participation-enhancing rather than preventive-equivalent, given its limited sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions [P6].

**(c) Early-onset CRC etiology.** The relative contribution and causal importance of life-course environmental, metabolic, inflammatory, and microbial exposures interacting with inherited susceptibility and birth-cohort effects "remain incompletely defined" [P9].

**(d) Screening–diagnostic pathway linkage.** Because of CRC's "silent early evolution," screening "must be tightly linked to structured diagnostic pathways" — a linkage the evidence frames as a requirement rather than a solved problem [P4].

## 4. Items flagged as missing — explicit treatment

**P5 (Introduction).** This passage establishes the scale against which screening effects must be judged: CRC ranks third in incidence and second in cancer-related mortality, with ~2 million new cases and >900,000 deaths annually [P5]. It also lists persistent challenges — a "relatively low early diagnosis rate," drug resistance, and limited immunotherapy response — that constrain outcome improvement independent of screening [P5]. Notably, P5 does **not** make any claim about screening reducing incidence; its contribution here is burden framing and the early-diagnosis gap.

**P3 (Background).** P3 reports that CRC is the third most commonly diagnosed malignancy "with increasing incidence and mortality rates" [P3]. This is in tension with the incidence-reduction claims in P1/P2/P9 and should be read as a global/aggregate statement rather than a contradiction of the older-adult, high-income-program effects; P3 states no population, region, or time window for its trend claim (not stated). P3 contains no screening-outcome data.

**P7 (Future Directions).** P7 concerns the gut microbiome and antitumor immunity, not screening. Its unresolved-questions content is that translation of microbiome-mediated immune regulation into routine practice "remains limited by methodological, biological, and regulatory challenges" [P7]. It does not address CRC incidence or screening; cited here only to record that it offers no screening evidence.

**P8 (Future research).** P8 addresses climate change, environmental exposures, and **breast** cancer, stating that important biological and epidemiological questions "remain unresolved" [P8]. It provides no colorectal cancer screening evidence and is not applicable to this question.

**P10 (Future perspectives).** P10 addresses bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) and the "driver–passenger problem" — whether disease-associated BEVs are primary drivers, secondary amplifiers, or passive reflections of dysbiosis [P10]. This is an unresolved causal-inference question in CRC biology, not a screening question; it does not report incidence effects of screening.

**F2.** No figure or table with the identifier F2 appears in the supplied evidence. I cannot cite or analyze it; this item is **not available** in the provided material.

## 5. Summary

# Traditional Adenoma–Carcinoma Model vs. Contemporary CRC Research

## 1. The traditional model (foundational framework)

The classical adenoma–carcinoma sequence describes colorectal tumorigenesis as cumulative molecular alterations unfolding over time [P1]. In the conventional sporadic model, early APC loss and Wnt-pathway activation are followed by additional alterations that can include KRAS activation, 18q loss (SMAD4/DCC), and TP53 inactivation, though the order is not invariant [P4]. Morphologically, this corresponds to progression from normal mucosa through a polypoid adenoma to invasive carcinoma, enabling colonoscopic detection and polypectomy [P4]. The sequence is characterized by stepwise genetic changes and chromosomal instability [P3], and remains an ideal disease model for studying stepwise metabolic reprogramming [P7]. Genetically engineered mouse models (e.g., ApcMin/+) have provided key insights into Wnt/β-catenin-driven initiation, with compound mutant models recapitulating the adenoma–carcinoma sequence [P9].

## 2. Why contemporary research considers it insufficient

Contemporary CRC research has shown that this framework, while foundational, is **insufficient to explain the biological diversity, clinical heterogeneity, and treatment resistance** observed in modern practice [P1]. High-throughput sequencing, single-cell analysis, spatial profiling, and microbiome research have recast CRC as a heterogeneous, adaptive, and multiscale disease [P1].

## 3. Key differences

**(a) Alternative evolutionary routes.** Beyond the conventional sequence, a serrated pathway is increasingly recognized, encompassing precursor lesions and carcinomas with characteristic morphology and molecular features; serrated adenocarcinoma and mismatch repair-deficient tumors are frequently associated with CIMP and MSI [P3]. In colitis-associated cancer (CAC), the inflammation–dysplasia–carcinoma sequence often inverts the genetic order: TP53 mutation/LOH can occur in non-dysplastic mucosa, whereas APC alterations occur later and less frequently than in sporadic CRC [P4].

**(b) Microbial ecology as a causal layer.** Contemporary work positions the intestinal microbiota as a key ecological factor, with "alpha-bug" and "driver–passenger" models, dysbiosis-linked genotoxins, barrier disruption, and immune modulation [P3]. Intratumoral microbial communities shift dynamically during progression—Proteobacteria decline while Firmicutes expand, and *F. nucleatum* rises from 5.9% in adenomas to 81.8% in advanced CRC [P10]. Shotgun metagenomics has identified compositional and functional differences across the adenoma–carcinoma sequence (e.g., *Bifidobacterium animalis* depletion in adenoma and CRC) [P6].

**(c) The immune-microenvironment dimension (missing item P8).** Contemporary research adds an immunological layer absent from the classical model. In microsatellite-stable (MSS) CRC, the gut microbiome acts as "an additional regulatory layer" superimposed on tumor-intrinsic, stromal, vascular, and metabolic mechanisms of immune resistance [P8]. *F. nucleatum* is a model organism here, linked to immune modulation, reduced cytotoxic activity of T and NK cells, and possible impairment of immunotherapy responsiveness in MSS CRC [P8]. This reframes CRC not merely as a genetic sequence but as an immunologically heterogeneous disease—a dimension the adenoma–carcinoma model does not capture.

**(d) Therapeutic and translational reframing (missing item P5).** The contemporary landscape extends beyond polypectomy and cytotoxic therapy. Evidence from botanical pharmacology illustrates this broader translational scope: *S. alexandrina* extracts show anticancer potential attributed to anthraquinone glycosides and flavonoids, with dose-dependent cytotoxic/antiproliferative activity across cancer cell lines [P5]. However, the evidence strength varies by indication—classified as direct experimental support, indirect mechanistic support, or traditional use not experimentally confirmed [P5]. This exemplifies how contemporary research evaluates candidate agents with graded evidence frameworks rather than a single linear disease model. (Note: this evidence concerns a medicinal plant, not CRC pathogenesis per se; its relevance is illustrative of expanded therapeutic investigation.)

**(e) Screening and biomarker paradigms.** Blood-based cfDNA screening has entered US regulated practice for average-risk adults ≥45 years, and ctDNA has prognostic and selected decision-support utility, though broader treatment-guiding utility remains under prospective evaluation [P1]. Microbiome-based predictors remain investigational [P6].

# Why Reproducibility Is a Central Challenge in AI Biomarker Discovery

## 1. It is identified as an unsolved, field-level problem
Reproducibility is explicitly framed as "one of the most significant unsolved challenges in AI-powered biomarker research" [P2], and as a challenge "repeatedly highlighted in translational biomarker research" [P1]. The core empirical pattern is that biomarkers performing well in discovery datasets "often show declines in accuracy, calibration, or clinical utility when evaluated across independent cohorts, health systems, or measurement platforms" [P2].

## 2. Sources of non-reproducibility in measured signals
Measured signals are "susceptible to cohort-specific effects, pre-analytical variability, platform drift, batch effects, and confounding factors related to concomitant diseases and treatment" [P1]. In multi-omics specifically, insufficient standardized protocols for sample collection, preprocessing, quality control, and cross-platform normalization "limit reproducibility across independent studies" [P4].

## 3. High dimensionality and analytical flexibility promote overfitting
High-dimensional feature domains "increase the risk of overfitting when sample sizes are modest and analytical flexibility is high" [P1]; high dimensionality frequently exceeds available sample sizes, "increasing the risk of overfitting and reducing model generalizability" [P4]. In discovery settings, "thousands of associated features may appear predictive, but only a subset will be stable under perturbation" [P7].

## 4. AI-specific failure modes that mimic good performance
Rich datasets "create new opportunities for bias and error": region-specific signatures, hidden confounding factors, and label leakage "can produce seemingly accurate models that fail when evaluated in independent cohorts or real-world settings" [P1]. Models may learn superficial correlations with strong developmental performance but "lack biological relevance and robustness" [P1]. In microbiome work, a model may have learned "batch, diet, medication, sequencing center, or geography rather than transferable biology," with apparent performance depending strongly on cohort structure, feature processing, and validation design [P3].

## 5. Transparency deficits compound the problem
AI-based biomarkers require explicit specification of cohort definition, endpoint labeling, preprocessing decisions, missing-data handling, model development choices, and evaluation protocols [P1]. "The fact that a lack of transparency weakens reproducibility has led to the development of AI-specific reporting frameworks and bias assessment tools" [P1].

## 6. Validation infrastructure is incomplete
Large consortia, benchmark datasets, and multicenter validation initiatives "often fail to fully reflect the diversity and complexity of real-world clinical settings" [P2]. Prospective validation in large, ethnically diverse cohorts "remains limited, and many published biomarkers have not yet undergone external validation" [P4].

## 7. Why it matters: reproducibility is broader than discrimination performance
Predictive performance alone "is increasingly seen as insufficient"; instead, "reproducibility should encompass stability across populations, consistency across technical platforms, and the preservation of clinical utility in independent settings" [P2]. Unstable feature sets "weaken biological interpretation and render subsequent validation inefficient," and inter-site generalization is "more important than intra-cohort performance" [P7]. The contrast between discovery opportunity and risk of erroneous findings is described as "a central challenge in contemporary biomarker science" [P1].

# Nitric Oxide Synthesis by NOS Enzymes

## Core Catalytic Reaction

NOS enzymes catalyze the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO) from L-arginine and molecular oxygen in the presence of NADPH, generating L-citrulline as a coproduct [P1]. The reaction proceeds in two steps: L-arginine is first hydroxylated to N-hydroxy-L-arginine, which is subsequently oxidized to yield NO and L-citrulline [P1]. Active NOS functions as a homodimer, with each monomer comprising a reductase domain and an oxygenase domain; the enzymes contain covalently bound heme and the flavin cofactors FAD and FMN, and require tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), which sits between the two domains of a monomer but interacts with residues of the opposing monomer, contributing to dimer stabilization [P1]. Dimer formation is further stabilized by a Zn²⁺ ion coordinated by four cysteine residues, two from each monomer [P1]. NO synthesis requires cooperation between both monomers: electron transfer from NADPH proceeds through FAD and FMN in the reductase domain of one monomer to the heme iron in the oxygenase domain of the other monomer [P1]. Several mechanistic aspects of this reaction remain incompletely understood [P1].

## Isoenzyme-Specific Context of Synthesis

NOS1 and NOS3 require relatively high intracellular Ca²⁺ (~400 nM) and are therefore calcium-dependent, low-output isoenzymes under physiological cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ (~100 nM) [P1]. NOS2, by contrast, contains tightly bound calmodulin and requires approximately tenfold lower Ca²⁺ concentrations, so calcium availability is generally not limiting; NOS2 can thus produce large amounts of NO continuously for extended periods, often several hours, with synthesis ceasing only upon degradation of the enzyme protein [P1]. This high-output capacity is why NO production must be tightly regulated given its broad biological activity and potential cytotoxicity [P2].

## Assembly Requirements for Catalytically Active Enzyme

All NOS isoenzymes are synthesized as monomers, but their catalytically active form is a homodimer [P3]. Dimerization requires heme, L-arginine, and tetrahydrobiopterin, with tetrahydrobiopterin exerting a stronger stabilizing effect than L-arginine [P3]. Heme incorporation is ATP-dependent and facilitated by HSP90A; its inhibition (e.g., by radicicol) nearly abolishes NOS2 assembly [P3]. Among NOS isoenzymes, NOS2 forms the least stable dimers and is most prone to disassembly [P3]. Excessive NO production can inhibit NOS2 dimerization by limiting heme availability, and NO-derived species can interfere with dimer formation through coordination with heme Fe³⁺ after incorporation [P3]. Post-translational modifications—tyrosine nitration (Tyr299, Tyr336, Tyr446, Tyr698) and S-nitrosation of cysteine residues in the tetrathiolate zinc-binding motif—promote monomerization and loss of activity [P3]. Regulatory proteins such as NAP110 and kalirin bind the NOS2 N-terminus and prevent dimerization [P3], and PI3K supports NOS2 assembly, likely via tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis through GTP cyclohydrolase 1 induction [P3].

## Regulation of Synthesis at the Protein Level

Compared with other NOS isoenzymes, regulation of NOS2 at the protein level remains relatively understudied [P5]. Nevertheless, NOS2 activity is controlled through regulation of dimer assembly, subcellular localization, catalytic activity, and protein turnover, frequently modulated by protein–protein interactions and post-translational modifications including tyrosine nitration, S-nitrosylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and acylation [P5]. Unlike NOS1 and NOS3, NOS2 is controlled predominantly at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels rather than through modulation of enzymatic activity [P2]; in human cells, NOS2 induction typically requires combined microbial signals (e.g., LPS) and pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-1β [P2].

## Context-Dependent Consequences of the NO Produced

The biological effects of NOS-derived NO depend on its concentration, enzymatic and cellular source, and local microenvironment, spanning antioxidant/pro-oxidant, anti-/pro-inflammatory, cytoprotective/cytotoxic, anti-/pro-apoptotic, and antifibrotic/profibrotic actions [P2]. The low NO amounts from constitutive NOS1/NOS3 have long been associated with physiological functions, whereas high-output NOS2-derived NO during inflammation has traditionally been regarded as pro-inflammatory; however, growing evidence indicates that the consequences of NOS2 activation are highly context dependent and cannot be explained by a simple constitutive-versus-inducible distinction [P2]. Regulation of NOS2 extends substantially beyond the classical IFNγ/STAT1 and NF-κB pathways, with epigenetic mechanisms, microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, mRNA stability, protein turnover, and intracellular trafficking shaping the magnitude, duration, and consequences of NO production [P4]. NOS2 is also distributed heterogeneously across epithelial, stromal, endothelial, and immune-cell populations with non-equivalent functions [P4].

## Uncoupled NOS: An Alternative Reaction Outcome

When the substrate L-arginine or the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin is limited, endothelial NOS uncouples and reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide instead of producing NO [P6]. Uncoupling is rarely complete, so the same enzyme can produce NO and superoxide together, which combine at a near diffusion-limited rate to form peroxynitrite [P6]. Consistent with the substrate dependence of NO synthesis, NO is described as synthesized from L-arginine in vascular endothelial cells under the catalysis of eNOS [P7].
