## 1. General decision framework (not HCC-specific)

The evidence base for rechallenge is derived primarily from retrospective cohorts with selection bias and confounding by indication; reported recurrence rates vary widely (30–50%) and predictors of recurrence are not well-defined. The decision "ultimately depends on multiple patient-specific, tumor-specific, and treatment-specific factors, and there is no validated risk stratification tool to guide this decision" [P3]. ## 2. irAE-type–specific determinants

- **Audiovestibular/ototoxicity:** No literature exists to guide patient selection for rechallenge after ototoxicity; NCCN suggests resuming ICI for grade 2–3 irAEs improving to at least grade 1, but makes no ototoxicity-specific recommendation. # Conditions for Calling an AI Biomarker Clinically Useful

## 1. Evidence-maturity thresholds (validation hierarchy)

Published claims often fail to distinguish exploratory associations from clinically applicable tools [P7]. Progression requires: external validation in independent cohorts (different locations, time periods, or clinical contexts), since external replication alone does not guarantee clinical significance if patient spectrum, treatment models, or outcome definitions differ from intended use; prospective validation with pre-specified data collection, endpoints, and analysis plans; and evidence of clinical benefit—whether biomarker-guided decisions improve patient outcomes or resource allocation versus standard care, assessed via decision curve analysis, net utility frames, pragmatic trials, or embedded application studies [P7]. Finally, regulatory and clinical adoption evidence must reflect sustained real-world performance, workflow integration, and post-market oversight, with lifecycle oversight for adaptive systems [P7]. Progression is not guaranteed: many biomarkers with strong exploratory performance fail at external or prospective evaluation due to biological heterogeneity, dataset shift, or practice changes [P7].

## 2. Analytical, clinical, and utility validity plus governance

Table 11 specifies what must be validated, by whom, and typical failure points: analytical validity (assay + preprocessing; laboratory + vendor; accuracy, reproducibility; failure = batch effects); clinical validity (biomarker–outcome correlation; developers; external cohorts; failure = spectrum bias); clinical utility (decision benefit; trial sponsors; interventional trials; failure = no impact on workflow); algorithm governance (model stability; manufacturers; version control audits; failure = drift post-distribution); and post-marketing surveillance (safety and bias; institutions; real-world monitoring; failure = recalibration neglected) [P6]. Meeting these is vital not only for regulatory approval but for sustainable clinical reliability in environments with adaptive models and evolving data distributions [P6].

## 3. Mechanistic grounding versus correlational fragility

Most AI-derived biomarkers are correlational by construction; while correlational biomarkers are clinically useful, they are fragile when used to guide treatment, predict response mechanisms, or serve as surrogate endpoints [P3]. Mechanistic interpretation should integrate computational evidence with biological plausibility, perturbation consistency, and pathway coherence rather than relying solely on pattern explainability, since feature attribution without such integration risks compelling narratives unsupported by causal biology [P3]. Biological validity and mechanistic grounding are central when biomarkers inform therapeutic development, patient stratification, or treatment selection [P8].

## 4. Real-world evidence and post-implementation monitoring

After transition to clinical practice, AI biomarkers must be evaluated under real-world conditions of heterogeneous populations, evolving practice, and variable data quality [P1]. RWE can assess whether biomarker-guided decisions improve outcomes, reduce costs, or change treatment models versus standard care; post-application monitoring should evaluate prediction performance plus clinical impact, adverse events, and equity among subpopulations, with recalibration or retraining under regulatory oversight when drift, test changes, or epidemiological shifts degrade performance [P1]. RWE can also refine thresholds, decision rules, and patient selection by revealing discrepancies between trial performance and real-world efficacy [P1]. Ultimately, successful implementation depends not only on predictive accuracy but on demonstrable improvements in patient outcomes, treatment selection, and healthcare delivery [P1].

## 5. Workflow integration and interpretability thresholds

Even analytically validated biomarkers can fail clinically if they cannot be integrated into routine workflows [P9]. Practical application requires compatibility with laboratory information systems, imaging platforms, and electronic health records, plus clearly defined clinical action thresholds; translating continuous risk scores into actionable categories remains one of the biggest adoption barriers [P9]. Interpretability requirements are context-dependent—mechanistic transparency may not be necessary for low-risk screening tools, while therapeutic decision support often requires description of contributing features or biological pathways; over-reliance on post-annotations lacking biological basis can create false reassurance [P9]. Clinician trust depends on perceived alignment with standards of clinical reasoning and evidence, not model performance alone [P9].

## 6. Disease-specific caveats (neurodegeneration)

AI-powered biomarkers support early diagnosis, prognostic stratification, disease classification, and longitudinal monitoring [P5]. However, characterizing them as surrogate endpoints is insufficient and limits their role in regulatory decision-making; the fundamental adoption barrier is biological and clinical heterogeneity (mixed pathologies, comorbidities, population diversity), and many models trained on select datasets fail in community settings [P5]. Reliable practice therefore requires consistent testing and imaging protocols, representative validation cohorts, and demonstration that biomarker-driven strategies improve not only diagnostic accuracy but clinical decision-making [P5].

## 7. Accountability and clinician responsibility

AI biomarkers distribute responsibility among algorithm developers, data providers, and institutions; regulatory and legal frameworks increasingly require documentation of intended use, decision-support limitations, and clinician override mechanisms, with clinicians retaining ultimate responsibility for patient care decisions [P6].

## 8. Explicitly stated prerequisite conditions in the source literature

- **Mitochondrial biomarker context:** clinical utility must be demonstrated rather than assumed—a useful test must classify a reproducible biological phenotype, predict prognosis or treatment response, and improve outcomes when used to guide care; until then, such biomarkers should remain research tools [P10].
- **SEM context (methodological analogy):** validity depends on all specified relationships being theoretically justified, measurement models demonstrating reliability and validity, and structural relationships being linear unless explicitly modeled otherwise [P4]. *(Note: this is a general statistical-modeling condition, not an AI-biomarker-specific criterion; it is cited here only as the source's stated validity conditions.)*
- **MR context (methodological analogy):** accurate causal estimation requires relevance, exchangeability, and exclusion restriction [P2]. *(Note: these are instrumental-variable conditions for Mendelian randomization, not AI-biomarker criteria; included only because the source states them as required conditions.)*

## 9. Summary of the source's own synthesis

Translational success depends as much on study design, validation strategy, and clinical integration as on algorithmic performance; common pitfalls include assuming statistical association has therapeutic significance, relying solely on endogenous cross-validation, and neglecting population diversity and health-system variability [P8]. Standardized evaluation frameworks should assess predictive performance plus robustness, calibration, fairness, and clinical utility [P8]. If these conditions are met, AI-powered biomarkers can evolve from exploratory research outputs into reliable components of therapeutic development and routine clinical decision-making [P8].

# Four ICI Rechallenge Strategies and the Observed ORR Difference

## The four strategies and their ORRs

Four combination strategies were defined by the pairing of initial and rechallenge regimens [P1]:

| Strategy | Initial ICI | Rechallenge | n (%) | ORR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | anti-PD-1 | targeted + anti-PD-L1 | 138 (36.0%) | 17.4% |
| 2 | targeted + anti-PD-L1 | ipilimumab + nivolumab | 100 (26.1%) | 18.0% |
| 3 | bevacizumab + atezolizumab | tremelimumab + durvalumab | 132 (34.5%) | 6.8% |
| 4 | bevacizumab + atezolizumab | same regimen (bevacizumab + atezolizumab) | 13 (3.4%) | 15.0% |

(All values from [P1]; the four-strategy taxonomy is also summarized in [P2].)

## Relationship to the ORR difference

The review attributes the ORR gap to the *drug-selection logic* of each strategy rather than to rechallenge per se: strategies 1 and 2 "achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable clinical outcomes than" strategies 3 and 4 [P1]. Strategy 1 (switching an anti-PD-1–pretreated patient to targeted therapy plus anti-PD-L1) is described as conferring clinical benefit with manageable safety, including one CR after initial pembrolizumab failure [P1]. Strategy 2 is characterized as providing "moderate activity, especially for patients pretreated with PD-L1-based regimens" [P1]. Strategy 3, by contrast, "displays a limited efficacy" despite offering "an alternative immunologic modulation," and carries the highest grade ≥3 irAE rate (24.3%) [P1]. Strategy 4 — the only same-regimen rechallenge evidence — shows "modest" efficacy in a very small, selected cohort (n = 13) [P1].

## Critical caveats on the ORR comparison

- **No statistical comparison was performed.** The review states explicitly that "no statistical comparisons have been performed across regimens among the different studies," that the evidence is mainly retrospective studies and case reports with "substantial heterogeneity," and that findings "should be interpreted with caution" [P1]. The ORR differences are therefore descriptive, not tested.
- **Pooled ORR differs from strategy-level ORRs.** The overall rechallenge ORR is reported as 13.8% in the abstract-level pooled analysis [P6] versus 17.4% in the regimen-level analysis [P1]; this discrepancy is not reconciled in the evidence and likely reflects different study sets (12 vs. 10–12 studies) — the source does not state the reason.
- **Strategy 4's ORR rests on a single study** of 13 patients [P1], so its apparent intermediate position (15.0%) is not comparable in precision to strategies 1–3.

## Why the ORR difference cannot yet be attributed to strategy choice

- **Rechallenge decisions are individualized, with no validated stratification tool** [P4]; the evidence base is retrospective with "significant selection bias and confounding by indication" [P4]. This applies directly to the strategy-level ORRs, since regimen assignment was not randomized [P1].
- **Interval length is a competing explanatory variable.** Rechallenge at an interval >1 month yielded ORR 19.1% and DCR 62.5%, versus ORR 20.0% and DCR 40.0% at <1 month [P7]. Because interval was not balanced across strategies in the evidence provided, it cannot be excluded as a driver of the ORR pattern; the review itself notes no definitive conclusion on timing [P7].
- **Patient factors** (preserved liver function, age <60, lower tumor burden) are associated with more frequent benefit and may confound strategy comparisons [P2].
- **General feasibility** of rechallenge for selected HCC patients is supported [P5], but this does not validate one strategy over another.

## Evidence gaps relevant to the ORR question

- **No head-to-head randomized data** exist comparing rechallenge strategies, or rechallenge versus TKIs, in HCC; the only randomized signal cited (CONTACT-03, renal cell carcinoma) found rechallenge not superior to TKI [P3].
- **Predictive biomarkers** (tertiary lymphoid structures, ctDNA, B2M/CTNNB1 alterations) that might explain differential ORR across strategies remain unvalidated in HCC rechallenge [P3].
- **Safety mitigation strategies** after rechallenge, including for pneumonitis, are identified as unstudied [P8]; this is relevant because strategy 3's limited efficacy coincides with its higher toxicity [P1].
- **Microbiome-directed adjuncts** are not established for improving ICI efficacy and should not be used outside trials [P9]; they therefore cannot currently be invoked to explain or modify the strategy-level ORR differences.

## Bottom line

The observed ORR difference tracks the initial-to-rechallenge drug pairing: strategies that switch mechanism (1 and 2) show higher ORR (17.4%, 18.0%) than same-class CTLA-4/PD-L1 switching (3; 6.8%) or same-regimen rechallenge (4; 15.0%, n = 13) [P1]. However, this ranking is descriptive only — no statistical comparison was performed, heterogeneity and selection bias are substantial [P1, P4], and interval [P7] and patient factors [P2] are uncontrolled confounders. The evidence is insufficient to establish a causal link between strategy choice and ORR.

# EV Subpopulations in Breast Cancer Metastasis and Diagnosis

## 1. Subpopulation Classification

In BC, distinct EV subpopulations—mainly small EVs (sEVs), large EVs (lEVs), and apoptotic bodies—play distinct roles in promoting tumour progression and metastasis [P1]. Size-based categories are used per MISEV guidelines: sEVs/exosomes ~50–200 nm, lEVs ~150–500 nm, apoptotic bodies ~500–4000 nm; the authors caution that size ranges overlap and isolation methods may co-recover non-vesicular particles, so sEV/lEV are not used interchangeably with exosome/microvesicle [P1].

## 2. Contributions to Metastasis

### sEVs
- **General mechanisms:** sEV RNAs promote metastasis via increased endothelial permeability, EMT induction, immune modulation, and pre-metastatic niche (PMN) formation [P2].
- **Macrophage reprogramming/TAM polarisation:** sEV miR-33, miR-130, and circ-0100519 activated TAMs [P2]; sEV miR-138-5p promoted TAM-like polarisation via KDM6B suppression, facilitating TNBC lung metastasis [P2]; sEV miR-21 (with RAB5A-enhanced secretion) suppressed PELI1 to promote TAM-like polarisation, and suppressed PDCD4 in osteoclast precursors to support a bone metastatic niche [P2].
- **Immune evasion:** sEV miR-27a-3p suppressed MAGI2, weakening PTEN-mediated PI3K/AKT inhibition and increasing PD-L1, enabling immune evasion [P2]; sEV circ-PSMA1 sponged miR-637 to activate AKT1/β-catenin signalling and enhance TNBC metastasis [P2].
- **Fibroblast crosstalk:** TNBC sEV miR-125b and miR-370-3p drove CAF differentiation; CAF-derived sEV miR-500a-5p and miR-18b enhanced metastatic features in BC cells [P2].
- **Vascular remodelling:** sEV miR-105 inhibited ZO-1, disrupting the endothelial barrier [P2].
- **Invasion/migration:** sEV miR-222 (via PDLIM2 suppression) and miR-10b (via HOXD10 suppression) promoted invasion/migration [P2]; lncRNA NEAT1 (sponging miR-141-3p/KLF12) and MALAT1 (via miR-1-3p/VASP) facilitated metastasis [P2].
- **Organotropism:** sEVs are associated with lung, liver, brain, and bone metastasis (e.g., miR-200 lung; miR-4443 liver; miR-1246/miR-1290/miR-301a-3p/GS1-600G8.5 brain; miR-940/miR-19a/IBSP bone) [P2][P7].
- **Proteins:** sEV cargoes include Ezrin, annexin A5/A6, tenascin, and EMMPRIN/CD147 [P4]; Table 2 lists sEV proteins such as Caveolin-1, CEMIP, EDIL3, EPHA2, ICAM1, integrins, Survivin, TSP1, and TβRII with graded evidence levels [P7].

### lEVs
- PD-L1-positive lEVs from TNBC patients suppressed cytotoxic T-cell activity and promoted M2-like macrophage polarisation via TBK1/STAT6 [P7]; irradiation induced PD-L1-containing lEV release [P7].
- lEV CD44 reduced focal adhesions and induced actin cytoskeleton rearrangement, enhancing metastatic potential of low-metastatic BC cells [P7].
- Tg2-enriched lEVs activated fibroblasts and increased tumour stiffness [P7]; chemotherapy increased phosphatidylserine-exposing lEVs that promoted platelet activation, endothelial permeability, and transendothelial migration [P7].
- lEVs are positioned as critical mediators with distinct properties, though studied less extensively than sEVs [P7].

### Comparative emphasis
sEVs appear more associated with organotropism and PMN conditioning; lEV involvement becomes more evident under therapy-induced stress [P7]. Overlapping protein content exists between subpopulations, with some proteins (e.g., metabolic enzymes) enriched in lEVs [P7]. Migrasomes (~500 nm–3 μm) are noted, but current isolation cannot reliably distinguish them from lEVs, so functional effects attributed to migrasomes may involve co-isolated lEVs [P7].

## 3. Diagnostic/Biomarker Potential

- EVs reflect the molecular composition of their cell of origin and are abundant in body fluids, serving as messengers in cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis [P1].
- Growing evidence highlights EVs as potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets [P5].
- **sEVs:** multiple circulating RNAs and proteins evaluated in clinical samples (e.g., serum NEAT1 highly expressed in BC patients [P2]; sEV miR-7641 elevated in plasma of patients with distant metastasis [P2]; sEV miR-361-3p positively correlated with malignancy in plasma [P2]; sEV miR-199b-5p higher in brain-metastasis patients [P2]) [P7].
- **lEVs:** emerging potential but limited clinical evidence [P7].
- Subtype-specific lipid profiles may provide additional biomarkers for BC detection and classification, though further studies are required [P7].
- Single-EV analysis (nano-flow cytometry, droplet-based assays, Raman spectrometry, aptamer-based detection, single-EV imaging) may resolve heterogeneity and support clinically useful EV-based biomarkers [P1].

## 4. Caveats Stated in the Evidence

- EV size ranges overlap and isolation methods may co-recover non-vesicular particles [P1]; current isolation lacks resolution to reliably distinguish EV subtypes [P7].
- For RNA cargoes in Table 1, vesicular delivery is "plausible, but in most cases, not formally demonstrated"; phenotypes could involve non-EV carriers [P2].
- Clinical translation remains challenging (Phase I oncology success ~3.4%) [P1].

# Why ctDNA Is Attractive in HCC and the Clinical Gap It Addresses

## 1. The core clinical gap: precision medicine without tissue

HCC is the most common primary liver cancer (~80% of cases), and many patients are diagnosed at advanced stages [P1]. Although targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors have made individualized precision medicine based on tumor characteristics increasingly important, **tumor tissue biopsy is not required for HCC diagnosis, which makes precision medicine more challenging** [P1]. This is the central gap: routine tissue-based genomic profiling is lacking in HCC, and tissue-informed assays (e.g., minimal residual disease assays such as Signatera®) may have limited applicability in advanced HCC, which is often diagnosed without biopsy-confirmed tissue [P2].

## 2. Why ctDNA is attractive

- **Noninvasive and safe alternative:** Liquid biopsy profiles ctDNA shed from tumors into circulation and "may provide a noninvasive and safe alternative for cancer genomic profiling and thus compensate for the lack of routine tissue-based genomic profiling in HCC" [P1].
- **Clinically acceptable concordance with tissue:** In 130 patients with advanced HCC, overall concordance among key genes showed 72.6% sensitivity and 75.0% PPV (64.3%/67.9% including TERT promoter mutations), consistent with prior large solid-tumor studies [P2]. Restricting to sampling intervals ≤30 days improved sensitivity to 96.3% [P2].
- **Prognostic value of maxVAF:** This is the first study to demonstrate the prognostic value of ctDNA maxVAF in a large advanced-HCC cohort treated with atezo/bev; maxVAF remained an independent prognosticator for PFS and OS after adjusting for clinical factors, and was associated with treatment response and survival in the atezo/bev group [P2]. ctDNA mutations in TP53 and TERT were more significantly associated with poor survival than tumor tissue mutations [P2].
- **Complementary role:** ctDNA is positioned as "a noninvasive and complementary technique for genomic profiling in advanced HCC, particularly when tissue-based sequencing is not feasible" [P2].

## 3. Required additional evidence items

**[P7] — The population in which ctDNA was evaluated:** The cohort comprised 130 advanced HCC patients (median age 61 years; 83.8% male), with extrahepatic spread in 77.7% and PVTT in 23.1%; baseline AFP exceeded 400 ng/mL in 38.5%, and 86.2% were BCLC stage C; 69.2% had HBV etiology, and 73.1% received atezo/bev first-line [P7]. This characterizes the advanced, largely HBV-related population in which ctDNA was shown to be feasible — a limiting condition for generalizability (the authors note the cohort was exclusively East Asian from an HBV-endemic region and requires external validation [P2]).

**[P6] — The surveillance/diagnostic gap at the health-system level:** In the Saudi cohort, the relatively high proportion of patients presenting with advanced tumor burden underscores the need to strengthen surveillance, and current guidelines recommend regular screening with imaging and serum biomarkers, yet adherence remains variable [P6]. The frequent presentation with advanced features (vascular invasion, portal vein thrombosis) mirrors concerns about delayed diagnosis and limited eligibility for curative therapies [P6]. This is a regional, real-world illustration of the late-diagnosis gap that noninvasive molecular approaches are intended to address — though [P6] does not itself evaluate ctDNA.

**[P8] — Cautionary context on liquid-biopsy-type biomarkers in HCC:** For exosomal circRNAs and lncRNAs, the majority of reported mechanisms have been established in individual cell-line or animal models, and independent validation across HCC etiologies and clinical cohorts remains limited due to the lack of large-scale prospective studies, standardized detection methods, and multicenter clinical validation [P8]. This is a limitation of exosomal RNA biomarkers specifically, not ctDNA, but it illustrates the broader validation gap facing liquid-biopsy candidates in HCC.

**[P9] — The therapeutic-target gap ctDNA does not close:** HCC outcomes remain suboptimal due to late-stage diagnosis, a paucity of tumor-specific therapeutic targets, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment [P9]. Even promising targets such as GPC3 show pronounced inter- and intra-tumoral expression heterogeneity, restricting patient eligibility [P9]. Consistent with this, the ctDNA study authors state that "because HCC lacks established druggable targets, the therapeutic utility of ctDNA remains limited, and prognostic biomarkers, like maxVAF, must be further validated in larger, independent cohorts as predictive tools" [P2].

**[F2] — Clinical readiness tiering:** Per the cited text describing Figure 2, clinical readiness varies across the HCC treatment continuum: established clinical assessment remains the basis of treatment selection, whereas radiomics, ctDNA, molecular and immune profiling, AI, and digital pathology **remain investigational** [P4]. Investigational technologies are intended to complement, not replace, guideline-based assessment, with value determined by prospective validation [P4]. *(Note: the figure itself is not included in the evidence; this is drawn from the passage describing it.)*

## 4. Summary

ctDNA is attractive in HCC because it offers a noninvasive, tissue-free route to genomic profiling precisely where tissue profiling is not routine [P1], with clinically acceptable tissue concordance [P2] and independent prognostic value of maxVAF in atezo/bev-treated advanced HCC [P2, P7]. The gap it addresses is the absence of routine tissue-based genomic profiling in a cancer often diagnosed at advanced stage without biopsy [P1, P2, P6]. However, its therapeutic utility remains limited by the lack of druggable targets in HCC [P2, P9], and it remains an investigational, complementary tool pending prospective validation [P4].

# Moving AI Biomarkers from Promising Results to Clinical Practice

## 1. Rigorous validation beyond statistical performance
The transfer of candidate biomarkers to practice is "disproportionately limited compared to their discovery output," reflecting "weaknesses in validation processes rather than technological capability" [P1]. Reproducibility is undermined by cohort-specific effects, pre-analytical variability, platform drift, batch effects, and confounding, with overfitting risk heightened in high-dimensional, modest-sample settings [P1]. Crucially, evaluation often relies on discrimination (AUC) "without demonstrating whether the biomarker actually improves patient management or outcomes," highlighting the distinction between statistical performance and clinical benefit [P1]. Translation therefore "demands rigorously validated development processes, transparent reporting, and documented clinical benefit" [P1]. AI-specific reporting frameworks and bias assessment tools are needed because "a lack of transparency weakens reproducibility" [P1].

## 2. A structured, multi-phase development pipeline
An integrated workflow spans four interconnected phases—Discovery, Validation (external cohort testing, TRIPOD + AI compatibility, systematic bias assessment), Clinical utility (decision curve analysis, net benefit quantification, workflow integration), and Therapeutic integration (accompanying diagnostic development, trial enrichment, response monitoring)—with iterative refinement cycles based on clinical feedback [F2]. In the clinical utility phase, biomarkers "should demonstrate incremental decision value according to established workflows, quantified through decision analytics that translate predictions into actual patient outcomes," particularly where incremental value must be defined by decision point and patient subgroup [P1].

## 3. Mechanistic grounding and biological interpretation
Moving "from purely predictive markers to biologically based and therapeutically applicable biomarkers requires the explicit integration of mechanistic modeling and validation" [P7]. Correlation-based biomarkers "provide predictive signatures but are often lack biological interpretability," whereas mechanistically informed biomarkers integrate biological context, causal reasoning, and pathway-level understanding to better support therapeutic decision-making [P7]. Realizing this requires "careful separation of correlational signatures from causal or actionable mechanisms through biological validation and orthogonal experiments" [P1].

## 4. Coordinated validation across analytical, algorithmic, and workflow dimensions
"Effective use of AI biomarkers requires coordinated validation of analytical tests, algorithms, and clinical workflows" [P5]. Table 11 specifies requirements, responsible parties, typical evidence, and common failure points: analytical validity (analysis + preprocessing; laboratory + vendor; accuracy/reproducibility; batch effects), clinical validity (biomarker–outcome correlation; developers; external cohorts; spectrum bias), clinical utility (decision benefit; trial sponsors; interventional trials; no impact on workflow), algorithm governance (model stability; manufacturers; version control audits; drift post-distribution), and post-marketing surveillance (safety and bias; institutions; real-world monitoring; recalibration neglected) [P5]. Meeting these is vital "not only for regulatory approval but also for sustainable clinical reliability" [P5].

## 5. Real-world evidence and post-implementation monitoring
After transition to practice, AI biomarkers "must be evaluated under real-world conditions characterized by heterogeneous populations, evolving clinical practices, and variable data quality" [P2]. RWE can assess whether biomarker-guided decisions improve outcomes, reduce costs, or change treatment models versus standard care; monitoring should cover clinical impact, adverse events, and equity, with recalibration or retraining under regulatory oversight to address model drift [P2]. RWE can also refine thresholds, decision rules, and patient selection by revealing discrepancies between trial and real-world efficacy, requiring governance balancing innovation with safety and transparency [P2]. Ultimately, success "will depend not only on predictive accuracy but also on demonstrable improvements in patient outcomes, treatment selection, and healthcare delivery" [P2].

## 6. Accountability and governance
AI biomarkers distribute responsibility among algorithm developers, data providers, and institutions; frameworks increasingly require documentation of intended use, decision support limitations, and clinician override mechanisms, with clinicians retaining ultimate responsibility and institutions ensuring comparable standards of evidence and safety [P5].

## 7. Domain-specific adoption barriers
In neurodegeneration, "one of the biggest obstacles to the widespread adoption of blood-based Alzheimer's biomarkers remains the practical application challenges," with biological and clinical heterogeneity (mixed pathologies, comorbidities, population diversity) as the fundamental barrier; reliable practice requires consistent testing and imaging protocols, representative validation cohorts, and demonstration of improved clinical decision-making, not just diagnostic accuracy [P6]. In multi-omics T1D work, barriers include insufficient standardized protocols, high dimensionality versus sample size, limited prospective validation in diverse cohorts, and limited model interpretability [P8]. For microbiome biomarkers, routine practice requires them to be "reproducible, interpretable, cost–effective and demonstrably superior to existing clinical tools" [P4].

## 8. Institutional research capacity (contextual evidence)
Bibliometric analysis of 118 institutions (≥20 papers) found the University of London led publication volume (337 papers), followed by Harvard (299), North Carolina (241), and the University of California (233); the University of California showed the highest citation count, H-index, and centrality, and has advanced AD biomarker and disease-mechanism identification using AI-based data mining [P3]. International collaboration was relatively weak, with most partnerships concentrated domestically [P3]—contextualizing the collaborative capacity needed for multicenter validation, though this source does not directly prescribe translation requirements.

## Summary
The evidence converges on: rigorous external validation and transparent reporting [P1]; a four-phase pipeline with decision-analytic clinical utility assessment [F2, P1]; mechanistic validation beyond correlation [P7, P1]; coordinated analytical/clinical/workflow validation with governance and surveillance [P5]; real-world evidence and equity monitoring [P2]; and domain-specific protocol standardization and interpretability [P6, P8, P4].

*Note: [P3] is a bibliometric study and does not itself specify translation requirements; it is cited here only for the institutional/collaboration context it reports.*
